articles.title: Quote of the day by Leonardo da Vinci: "Men of lofty genius sometimes accomplish the most when they work least, for their minds are occupied with their ideas...to which they afterwards give form."
articles.summary: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian Renaissance thinker, painter, sculptor, architect, mathematician, and engineer, who is popularly known for his
articles.body: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian Renaissance thinker, painter, sculptor, architect, mathematician, and engineer, who is popularly known for his exceptional works like the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper.But what makes his life even more interesting is the thousands of pages where he wrote and thought about novel ideas and thoughts which perhaps made his life more captivating after he passed away.He once talked of a profound idea that the inspiration behind our work or good ideas rarely comes when we are at our desk, staring at a screen and forcing it, they possibly hit the mind while we are either walking, washing dishes, waiting for a bus, or looking out of a window. Ideas has a funny habit of turning up when we stop chasing them.Yet most of us feel guilty when we pause. Isn’t that strange?Let’s dig in to find out what he exactly said and meant.Quote of the dayMen of lofty genius sometimes accomplish the most when they work least, for their minds are occupied with their ideas and the perfection of their conceptions, to which they afterwards give formWhat does the quote mean?Leonardo says that people of great genius sometimes achieve the most when they seem to work the least. Their minds are busy with ideas and with refining them, and afterwards they give those ideas a form. So, he meant to say that thinking is real work, even when nobody can see it.The line is nearly always credited to Leonardo, yet it does not come from his own notebooks. It comes from Giorgio Vasari's Lives of the Artists, which describes Leonardo painting The Last Supper in a Milan convent. Vasari kept coaxing him to finish because Leonardo would sometimes stand lost in thought for half a day. He then complained to the Duke, who gently urged Leonardo to work. Leonardo then explained that great minds sometimes accomplish the most when they work least, seeking out ideas that the hands later express.But it is important to note that Vasari was born in 1511 and Leonardo died in 1519, so Vasari was retelling a story he had heard, not one he saw, and an actual version of his account has been translated over the years, but the essence of his advice has hardly aged.Making anything good has two stages: imagining and doing.It is interesting that the ‘doing’ part, like a brush on a wall, is the part people see, gets the credit. But the imagining that happens quietly in the head rarely does, and Leonardo's point was that rushing the quiet part spoils the result.How are his words relevant today?We often reward and appreciate those people who look busy, and feel guilty when we do not do anything productive. Many workplaces still count hours instead of results. Yet most of us have noticed that the answer to a stubborn problem often arrives in the shower, on a walk, or after a night's sleep.So the next time you feel guilty for pausing, ask yourself: am I avoiding the work, or preparing for it!You use AI every day. articles.title: A rare Canadian computer was forgotten in an Edmonton barn for decades; its first known unboxing came nearly 45 years after it was built
articles.summary: A rare Canadian-built computer that spent decades forgotten in a rural barn near Edmonton is preparing for a unique second chapter.
articles.body: A rare Canadian-built computer that spent decades forgotten in a rural barn near Edmonton is preparing for a unique second chapter. The AES Alphaplus 12, believed to have been built around 1981, had resurfaced in its original shipping box and was taken to Carleton University in Ottawa for a scheduled public unboxing. The machine has attracted attention because so little documentation exists about this particular model, leaving its internal components and configuration uncertain. Its discovery offered a rare opportunity to examine a little-known part of Canada's early computing history.Importance of the rare Canadian computer discovery in an Edmonton barnThe rediscovery of the AES Alphaplus 12 is significant not simply because an old machine survived for decades, but because so little is known about the exact model. According to Carleton University's School of Computer Science, the computer remained untouched after its time at the Northern Alberta Institute of Technology (NAIT) before being forgotten in a rural Edmonton barn.The university's announcement, published on 2 September 2026, described the machine as a rare example of Canadian computing heritage. The 2 October unboxing event was scheduled to give specialists an opportunity to identify and assess the machine, and also to establish what can be learned from the surviving hardware.The university also noted that the machine was sealed in its dusty shipping box. That condition made the discovery particularly intriguing, as its contents had not yet been examined in the context of the planned public unboxing.What made AES Data an important name in Canadian computingThe story of the Alphaplus 12 is closely connected to the development of electronic word processing in Canada. Carleton University's background article identifies Montreal-based AES Data Ltd. as the company behind the machine and traces its design lineage to the earlier AES-90.The AES-90 was an important development because it used a screen to display and edit text electronically. According to Carleton, it introduced capabilities such as automatic line wrapping, text justification and numerical alignment at a time when these functions were far from standard. In 1972, the press described the machine as an electronic editor, reflecting how different it was from conventional typing equipment.By 1978, AES was competing directly with IBM as Canada's largest word-processing supplier, according to the university's account. The company was acquired by Ottawa's Kinburn Technology Corporation in 1987, creating a further connection between its history and the city where the newly recovered machine was taken.How much is known about the Alphaplus 12 todayDespite AES Data's importance in the word-processing industry, information about the Alphaplus 12 itself remains remarkably scarce. Carleton's School of Computer Science reported finding only 2 pieces of documentation relating specifically to the model. A listing in a British museum archive and a brief reference in a Canadian trade magazine from 1981.Even Ingenium, Canada's national science and technology museum, has early AES word processors and software in its collection but no record of this particular model, the university reported. That gap made the recovered machine especially valuable to researchers trying to establish a clearer picture of the country's computing history.A separate entry in the Time-Line Computer Archive provides some context about the wider Alphaplus family. Its listing for the AES Alphaplus 14 describes a word processor built in the early 1980s by the Montreal-based company. The archive explains that the machine was designed for word processing rather than as a general-purpose computer and features a printer built into the monitor.However, the archive documents the Alphaplus 14, not the recovered Alphaplus 12. Its description therefore offers background on related equipment, rather than proof of the exact features or configuration of the barn discovery.The unboxing at Carleton University took place on 2nd October at 2 pm in room 4155 of the Herzberg Building where a livestream was also planned, according to the university's announcement on 18 September 2026.A forgotten machine returns to Canada's computing historyCarleton's announcement places the discovery within a wider pattern of vintage-computing finds. The university's background article recalls the appearance of roughly 2,200 NABU computers from a barn in Massachusetts in 2023. Those machines had their own Canadian connection, having been developed by the Ottawa-based NABU Network in the early 1980s. It also describes the discovery of two Q1 microcomputers beneath boxes at Kingston University in London.The Alphaplus 12 is a smaller discovery in scale, but its limited documentation made it a unique find in its own right. Its journey from an educational institution in Alberta to decades of obscurity in a barn had left important details about the machine unresolved.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Drumcree: Michelle O'Neill receives PSNI investigation letter
articles.summary: The first minister says she will "co-operate with the investigation" into a protest over an Orange Order march in Portadown.
articles.body:
First Minister Michelle O'Neill has said she has received a letter from police investigating protests over the Drumcree parading dispute.

On Thursday, the police said they had begun issuing letters inviting people "reasonably suspected" of committing offences linked to the protests to interview.

Unionist politicians have called for action to be taken against O'Neill and other senior Sinn Féin politicians who took part in the protests against the Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road at the end of last month.

On Friday, Portadown deputy District Master Alastair Power said there would be "serious consequences" if the Northern Ireland Secretary intervenes to stop the march.

It is the 13th day of deadlock between residents of the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road and the local district lodge of the Orange Order.

The Parades Commission ruled that the march could go ahead with restrictions in place.

But the parade, from Drumcree Church into Portadown, did not happen due to a large protest on the Garvaghy Road.

O'Neill has previously defended her attendance at the protest, saying she was "proud to stand with the residents" and that "when the law is wrong, I will stand firmly against it".

The police statement did not name anyone they planned to issue a letter to.

In a statement issued by Sinn Féin on Friday afternoon, O'Neill confirmed she had received a letter from the PSNI.

"I can confirm I have received a letter inviting me for a police interview in relation to a peaceful protest on the Garvaghy Road. I will co-operate with the investigation," O'Neill said.

"For the last two weeks, I have stood in solidarity with the Garvaghy Road residents as attempts were made to force an unwanted Orange march through their community," she said.

"I will continue to stand with the Garvaghy Road residents who should be allowed to live in peace and free from sectarian intimidation," she added.

Earlier, Sinn Féin President Mary Lou McDonald said the party would "cooperate" in every way it could but that they remained "comfortable" in standing up for Garvaghy Road residents.

Sinn Féin MLA Deirdre Hargey also told the BBC that she had received a letter and would seek legal advice.

When asked by reporters on Friday how he would react if Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant intervenes and stops the Portadown District's parade going ahead, Power said they would "obviously not be very happy".

He said it would be the "first time the secretary of state has intervened on a lawful parade in over 30 years in overturning it".

"We're law abiding citizens and we will have to abide by the law but there will have to be serious consequences from the unionist community on that," he said.

Earlier, Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly, of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) told reporters she welcomed developments in the PSNI investigation, adding that the letters were "absolutely the right thing".

"It doesn't matter whether you are an ordinary citizen or first minister of the country, you have to be subject equally under the law."

Little-Pengelly also defended her attendance at the business engagement, after the DUP previously said it could not be "business as usual" at Stormont in response to Sinn Féin's involvement in protests on Garvaghy Road.

She said she did not want to punish "the work we need to do in terms of growing our economy and investing in public services... just because of the deeply reckless behaviour of Michelle O'Neill and Sinn Féin".

Speaking to The Nolan Show earlier, DUP leader Gavin Robinson said he expected "to see sanctions" for those investigated by the police.

Loyalist activist Jamie Bryson held a press conference on Friday, alongside DUP MP Carla Lockhart.

He said he had personal details published online on Thursday.

"I have received over 1,500 abusive calls, over 280 voicemails, many with threats to kill, to murder me, my family, people around me, and things have just reached a level now where it's totally unacceptable," he said.

Lockhart appealed to people to "step back" from making threats to her and Bryson.

She said: "People can fight us on our politics and our policies, and they may not like what we say and I'll take anyone on with regards to my politics.

"But when it gets personal and when you see and hear these threats online all it takes is for one person to just seriously think 'I really don't like those people' and I firmly believe it's getting to that point."

It is more than a week since the decision to allow an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road on Sunday, 27 September.

That morning, up to 1,000 people - including politicians such as O'Neill - blocked the road, preventing Orangemen marching from Drumcree Church a mile to the west.

Since then, residents have maintained a constant presence around the road while Orangemen have also repeatedly tried to march the route before being turned back by police.

The stand-off has caused considerable political fallout in Northern Ireland, with O'Neill facing a vote of no confidence over her involvement in the protest.

The vote is due to fail because it requires cross-community support at the Northern Ireland Assembly.

Drumcree was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading disputes, when stand-offs in the mid-to-late 1990s over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings.

When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.

The Parades Commission began operating in 1998 to regulate parades and try to defuse tension around marches.

Its decision not to allow a march down the Garvaghy Road that summer has been challenged by the order for the past three decades.

Earlier this year the Parades Commission decided that the march could go ahead with restrictions in place after its original decision to stop the march was overturned in court.

Meanwhile, the Court of Appeal is considering its ruling in a legal challenge brought by the residents to block the march going ahead.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia says three nationals killed in Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport.
articles.summary: The missile attacks come amid an escalation in fighting between the Iran-backed group and Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's government.
articles.body:
Three Saudi Arabian nationals have been killed in two attacks on the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, the country's civil aviation authority has said, after Yemen's Houthis said they had targeted the facility.

The attacks also resulted in "injuries to a number of Saudi citizens and residents of various nationalities", the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement on X.

It added that the first attack on Thursday targeted the airport while the second had struck an aircraft belonging to state carrier Saudia.

One of its pilots was among those killed, the airline said in a statement.

Air traffic had returned to normal, the civil aviation authority said.

Yemen's Houthi group said on Thursday it had attacked the airport with two ballistic missiles.

The Iran-aligned group said it had also targeted an airport in Najran city near the Saudi border with Yemen, and Khamis Mushait air base further north. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed these attacks.

The latest casualties follow the deaths of three people in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on 6 and 7 October.

Two were killed and 28 wounded in an attack at Abha International Airport, the civil aviation body said on Wednesday. Another person was killed at King Khalid airport in Riyadh.

The latest attacks come amid a marked escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west.

The Houthi military spokesman said the previous two attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports were in "response to the Saudi aggression against our country" that saw "60 air strikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours".

The group says it is targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war.

The conflict has worsened in recent weeks, after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.

That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping.

But Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.

A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.

A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

But the informal ceasefire began to unravel in July.

The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating against what they say is a years-long Saudi blockade and for an air strike on Sanaa airport.

articles.title: Japan protests Russia’s bid to extradite ICC top judge Tomoko Akane, a Japanese national, over Putin arrest warrant
articles.summary: Japan on Friday lodged a formal protest against Russia’s request for the extradition of International Criminal Court (ICC) President Tomoko Akane, a
articles.body: Japan on Friday lodged a formal protest against Russia’s request for the extradition of International Criminal Court (ICC) President Tomoko Akane, a Japanese national, from the Netherlands, describing the move as “unacceptable.”The protest came a day after Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office submitted extradition requests to the Netherlands, where the ICC is headquartered in The Hague, and several other countries for Akane and nine other ICC staff members.“Measures targeting individuals connected to the ICC are unjust and unacceptable. We regret that Russia made extradition requests to multiple countries nevertheless,” Japan’s deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki told reporters, according to the Associated Press.Tokyo would consider further action, including additional formal protests, Ozaki added.The requests followed Moscow’s issuance of arrest warrants for Akane and eight others in response to the ICC’s 2023 warrant for Russian President Vladimir Putin over the war in Ukraine. The Moscow City Court last year sentenced all nine in absentia to prison terms.Russia has accused the ICC of violating fundamental principles and norms of international law by issuing arrest warrants against Russian citizens without evidence, according to state news agency TASS.Relations between Japan and Russia have deteriorated since Putin visited the Kuril Islands, a Pacific island chain claimed by both countries, in August, marking his first visit to the archipelago. The Soviet Union seized the islands from Japan in the final days of World War II, and the dispute has prevented them from signing a peace treaty formally ending hostilities.Japan has also sought to balance its support for the ICC with its close ties to the United States, which opposes the court. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has faced domestic criticism over this balancing act.“We have consistently supported the ICC and will continue to do so,” Takaichi told parliament on Friday.Washington has accused the ICC of exceeding its mandate and imposed sanctions on Akane and about a dozen other court officials in retaliation for investigations into Israeli officials over the war in Gaza and probes into the conduct of US military personnel in Afghanistan.The sanctions freeze any assets held in US jurisdictions by those targeted and bar the officials and their family members from entering the United States.You use AI every day. articles.title: A French family found an 18th-century Chinese vase forgotten in an attic and carried it to Sotheby’s in a shoebox; after experts linked it to the Qianlong court, it sold for €16.18 million
articles.summary: An 18th-century Chinese porcelain vase that had been kept in the attic of a French family home was sold for €16.18 million at a Sotheby’s auction in Paris.
articles.body: An 18th-century Chinese porcelain vase that had been kept in the attic of a French family home was sold for €16.18 million at a Sotheby’s auction in Paris. The family had no idea how valuable the vase was when they brought it to the auction house wrapped in newspaper and placed inside an old shoebox. Experts later identified it as a rare piece made for the court of China's Qianlong Emperor.The vase had remained in the family for generations. According to Sotheby’s, it was among several Asian objects inherited from a relative who died in 1947. Although the family had preserved it, they did not particularly like its appearance. The owners reportedly considered it "too pink" and had left it in a box in the attic.Its value came to light when a woman contacted Sotheby’s Paris in March 2018. She had recently lost her husband and was preparing to move to the countryside. While clearing the house, she came across several objects of Asian origin and decided to ask whether they were worth examining.What followed was an unexpected discovery for the family. The vase, initially estimated at €700,000, eventually fetched €16,182,800 after a 20-minute bidding contest, setting a record at the time for Chinese porcelain sold at auction in France.From attic to Sotheby’sThe woman first spoke to Olivier Valmier, an Asian art specialist at Sotheby’s Paris, over the telephone. She described several objects in her possession, including a dragon robe, a censer, a mirror kept inside a lacquer box and a porcelain vase decorated with animals.She could not send photographs of the objects. However, Valmier became interested when she mentioned that the censer had an invoice connected to the 1867 Universal Exhibition in Paris.He asked her to bring the objects to Sotheby’s for examination. Initially, she hesitated because of the distance involved and worried that the journey might waste his time. Eventually, she agreed to bring one item, and Valmier selected the vase.Despite delays caused by train strikes, the woman arrived at the Paris office carrying the vase wrapped in crumpled newspaper, placed inside an old shoebox and covered with a plastic bag.When Valmier and his colleagues examined it, they immediately recognised its exceptional quality. Even if it had been a late 19th- or early 20th-century copy, they believed it could have been worth around €100,000.Further examination confirmed that it was an authentic 18th-century imperial porcelain vase, produced by the Jingdezhen workshops for the Qianlong Emperor's court. It was also in perfect condition. Describing the discovery, Valmier said, “It was as if we had just discovered a Caravaggio.”The vase’s rare featuresThe vase belonged to a rare category of Chinese porcelain known as Famille-Rose, or yangcai. These pieces are recognised for their detailed paintings, rich colours and complex production techniques.The vase, officially described as an Imperial 'Yangcai Crane and Deer Ruyi Vase', features a landscape painted around its body. The decoration includes nine fallow deer, five cranes, pine trees, rocky mountains and a waterfall.According to Sotheby’s, the deer, cranes and pine trees represent health and longevity in Chinese art. The landscape may also depict the vegetation of an imperial pleasure garden.Producing such porcelain required considerable skill and time. The detailed painting involved multiple layers of decoration, making these pieces particularly difficult to manufacture.Their rarity also contributed to their value. Sotheby’s explained that this type of porcelain was produced in extremely limited quantities, with most surviving examples now held in museums.Only one other vase of a comparable shape and design is known. That piece, which has different decorative details, belongs to the Musée Guimet in Paris.Connection with the Qianlong EmperorSotheby’s specialists also examined historical imperial records to understand the vase's origins. They found that an 18th-century imperial inventory listed two pairs of vases with designs matching the newly discovered piece.One pair had been commissioned in 1765 for a Buddha Hall, a space used for the emperor's private worship. Another pair was ordered in 1769 as a birthday gift.Although the exact history of the French family's vase before 1947 could not be established, these records helped experts connect its design to porcelain commissioned for the imperial court.Family documents showed that the vase had belonged to an uncle who died in 1947. His possessions included several Chinese and Japanese objects. The collection later passed through the family to the owners who brought the vase to Sotheby’s.The family's interest in Asian art may have extended further back. Records showed that an ancestor had received a Japanese Satsuma censer as a wedding gift, purchased at the 1867 Universal Exhibition in Paris.Sotheby’s suggested that the vase might have been acquired in Paris during the late 19th century, when Chinese and Japanese artworks were becoming popular among collectors.Sale reaches 23 times the estimateThe vase eventually went under the hammer at Sotheby’s Paris on June 12, 2018. Although its high estimate was €700,000, competition among bidders pushed the final price far beyond expectations.After approximately 20 minutes of bidding, the vase sold for €16,182,800, more than 23 times its high estimate. articles.title: Top Trump official mocked online over false claim of Indian stock market crash after US green card curbs
articles.summary: A top US official has faced online criticism after appearing to endorse a false claim that India's stock market had collapsed following the Trump
articles.body: A top US official has faced online criticism after appearing to endorse a false claim that India's stock market had collapsed following the Trump administration's latest restrictions on foreign workers, including Indian IT professionals.Anthony D'Esposito, Inspector General of the US Department of Labor, reacted to a post by American conservative commentator Benny Johnson on X with the words “Ruh roh”.The post claimed that India's stock market had “completely COLLAPSED” after the Trump administration suspended major technology companies from a programme linked to employment-based green cards.Social media users criticised the response, with some accusing the official of amplifying misinformation about India.On October 8, the Trump administration suspended eight major technology companies, including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe, from the Permanent Labor Certification, or PERM, programme.The move came amid the administration's broader efforts to curb what it alleges is the misuse of foreign worker programmes at the expense of American workers.PERM is a key step in the employment-based green card process. Employers seeking to sponsor most foreign workers for permanent residence must generally obtain certification from the Labor Department that there are not enough qualified, willing and available American workers for the position and that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect US wages and working conditions.What Benny Johnson claimed about Indian marketsReacting to the restrictions, Johnson claimed that the Indian stock market had crashed because of the administration's action against the tech companies.“The largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini were removed from the Permanent Labor Certification Program,” Johnson wrote on X.He also claimed that 75 per cent of Cognizant employees in the US were Indian nationals and pointed out that Infosys, Tata, Wipro and HCL were based in India.Johnson further alleged that these companies had sought millions of foreign workers over the years and questioned whether India's economy was based on “scamming” the US.However, a community note attached to Johnson's post pointed out that Indian stock markets had closed hours before the US administration announced the restrictions on October 8. This undermined the claim that the announcement had caused the market to crash that day.Users question US officialD'Esposito's brief response to Johnson's post prompted criticism from users who questioned why a senior US official appeared to engage with a claim contradicted by the community note.“How do you became inspector general, without even knowing the facts? Read the community notes,” one user wrote.Another user criticised the apparent amplification of the claim, writing: “Top US official is spreading fake news that Indian markets collapsed. And they have the gall to call Indians ‘scammers.’”While Indian benchmark indices fell sharply on Thursday, the decline was attributed to rising crude oil prices, the Reserve Bank of India's rate hike, and foreign investor outflows.On Friday, October 9, the Sensex and Nifty rebounded in early trade after two sessions of losses. The 30-share BSE Sensex rose 292 points to 71,876.10, while the NSE Nifty gained 84.60 points to 22,310.40.Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) shares surged more than 4 per cent after the company reported a 15 per cent year-on-year rise in net profit to Rs 13,884 crore. Infosys, HCL Tech and Tech Mahindra were also among the gainers.The controversy comes amid heightened scrutiny of Indian technology companies and foreign worker programmes under the Trump administration.The latest PERM suspensions could affect the green card sponsorship process for employees of the companies involved, although the move does not, by itself, mean that all their Indian employees have lost their jobs or visas.You use AI every day. articles.title: Alison Hammond: 'I thought I was having heart attack on air'
articles.summary: The host says a health scare on live TV was one of the "scariest things I've ever been through".
articles.body:
Alison Hammond has said she feared she was having a heart attack on air when she had to rush off ITV's This Morning midway through the programme last week.

The presenter appeared to clutch her chest as she left the show last Friday, and was taken to hospital to have a heart check-up.

She turned out to have suffered a panic attack, and said the experience was "probably one of the most scariest things I've ever been through".

Returning for her weekly slot on Friday, she told viewers: "I couldn't catch my breath and I genuinely thought I was having a heart attack. I'm so glad I'm here. I feel so grateful. I feel so thankful to God, to everything in life."

She added: "It felt like a heart attack. It was very real."

Alongside co-host Dermot O'Leary, Hammond introduced the programme by thanking him for holding the fort after her dramatic early exit, and also thanking everyone who sent good wishes.

She added: "It was the first time I've ever experienced anything like that. Secondly it was live on TV so I thought, oh my gosh, my son might be watching.

"So I just ran. I ran off TV. I would never do that normally but I just couldn't catch my breath."

The panic attack came on very quickly, she explained.

"It just was like a wave, something which I've now found out is adrenaline. That came into my body. I couldn't catch my breath and I genuinely thought I was having a heart attack."

The experience has given her a new perspective on life, she continued.

"I'm so happy that I'm here, and I'm so happy to see you," she said, putting both hands on Dermot's cheeks before hugging him.

"You were absolutely wonderful. And I'm so glad we're alive, and if anything it's made me look at life so much differently. Taking stock, look after my health. I'm drinking a lot of water."

The 51-year-old compared the feeling of the panic attack to crossing into a "surreal" place like the otherworldly Upside Down in TV show Stranger Things.

"I felt like I went into the other world - what's that show that I loved? Stranger Things. You know when you go into the Upside Down world? I felt like I went into the Upside Down world.

"I couldn't grasp my breath, and it was a panic attack."

Hammond and O'Leary also spoke further about panic attacks with former BBC Breakfast host and psychologist Dr Sian Williams, who has written a book about anxiety.

Hammond said she had been unsure about returning to This Morning - but felt that if she didn't come back this week, she may never do so.

"I'll be honest with you, I was anxious about coming back. But I thought, if I don't come back today, I probably wouldn't come back... because then I would have made a thing that it's This Morning that's causing the panic.

"But it can happen anywhere. It comes in ebbs and flows."

She and Williams also discussed the pressure of presenting live TV. "I do live TV all the time, I didn't realise it was having - I don't know if it was having an impact - the fact that you have to be 'on' in order to do it. I don't know," Hammond said.

She concluded the segment by telling viewers: "I'm back, babes. Keep rolling."

Earlier, looking ahead to the programme on ITV's Lorraine, Hammond had appeared to parody former This Morning presenter Holly Willoughby's 2023 monologue , which she famously began by asking viewers "are you OK?" in the wake of co-host Phillip Schofield's departure.

Hammond said on Lorraine: "I'm going to tell you everything, guys. Are you OK? I hope you are."

That line was met with laughter by Lorraine Kelly, who declared it "genius".

Hammond was taken to hospital after her departure from last Friday's episode of This Morning. She posted a video saying she was "getting my old ticker checked out" after what she described as "a little bit of a palpitation", which she hoped "was just a little panic attack".

She missed the Attitude Awards on Wednesday, where she won the The Honorary Gay Award.

The Birmingham-born presenter also hosts TV shows including The Great British Bake Off and For the Love of Dogs.

Also known as anxiety attacks, panic attacks can affect anyone, regardless of age, background or whether they have a history of anxiety.

Speaking on This Morning, Dr Williams described panic attacks as "anxiety on overdrive, when you can't find the reason".

They affect more women than men and can last between five and 20 minutes, she said. People experiencing one can "ground yourself" by focusing on the moment and the safety of their surroundings, and by steadying their breathing, she added.

"A heart attack and a panic attack are different, but they can feel the same because there are similar symptoms - choking or tingling or pain in the chest.

"If it's a heart attack it tends to radiate, so if might go down your arm or into your jaw. A heart attack doesn't subside with breathing or grounding in the same way."

According to the MIND mental health charity, panic attacks are an extreme anxiety response. They can develop quickly, and come with very intense symptoms.

articles.title: Jensen Huang and his wife Lori pledged $30 million to Stanford; in 2010, the university opened an engineering centre housing more than 270 faculty, staff and students, with workshops for building prototypes
articles.summary: Jensen Huang and Lori helped fund Stanford’s engineering centre with their $30 million donation.
articles.body: ​Jensen Huang and Lori helped fund Stanford’s engineering centre with their $30 million donation. The university dedicated the Jen-Hsun Huang Engineering Center as a shared space for research, education and collaboration across disciplines. The building houses more than 270 faculty members, staff and students, along with workshops for building prototypes and models.​The centre was established as part of Stanford’s Science and Engineering Quad, providing a shared space for students and researchers working across engineering, science and medicine. Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of Nvidia, received his master’s degree in electrical engineering from Stanford in 1992.​What is the Jen-Hsun Huang Engineering Center​The Jen-Hsun Huang Engineering Center was dedicated on October 5, 2010, as a new home for Stanford’s School of Engineering. The building was designed to serve as an academic and social destination for students and faculty, bringing together researchers from different departments and disciplines.​The centre houses members of the Department of Management Science and Engineering, the Institute for Computational and Mathematical Engineering and the Stanford Technology Ventures Program. It also accommodates the School of Engineering’s Dean’s Office and supporting departments.​The building features the 300-seat NVIDIA Auditorium and the Frederick Emmons Terman Engineering Library. The library was designed to support collaboration and help students and faculty access both digital and print research materials.​How the centre supports engineering research and innovation​The Huang Center was designed to encourage interaction between engineering researchers and colleagues in biology, chemistry, physics and medicine. Its open spaces, student lounges, and flexible furniture provide space for discussion and collaboration.​The building also includes workshops for constructing prototypes and models, allowing students to develop and test ideas. These facilities reflect the university’s approach to engineering education, which combines specialised technical knowledge with teamwork, communication, entrepreneurship and design.​At the centre’s dedication, Stanford President John Hennessy said the building "will foster future innovation and groundbreaking research for years to come."​Hennessy also thanked the Huangs for their support, saying their contribution reflected a tradition of alumni helping future generations access educational opportunities.​Why Jensen Huang supported the engineering centre​Huang said the project was intended to give students and teachers a place to work together and develop new ideas.​"To build a better future we must invest in tomorrow's innovators," Huang said. "There is no better place to do this than Stanford. Magic happens time and again when bright students learn together in an environment rich with faculty who are the best in their fields. With this new engineering center, we are giving students and teachers a place to collaborate and create our future. I hope that students will find inspiration here, and that Stanford will be as important in shaping their lives as it has been in mine."​The centre was also designed to address changes in engineering education. James D. Plummer, then dean of Stanford’s School of Engineering, said engineers needed to develop expertise in their fields while learning to work across disciplines and navigate a global economy.​The Huang Center's place in Stanford's campus​Located in the Science and Engineering Quad, the building forms part of Stanford’s broader campus plan, connecting the university’s historic Main Quad with newer science and engineering facilities.​Its design combines a modern interpretation of Stanford architecture with sustainability measures. The university said the Science and Engineering Quad buildings were designed to reduce potable water consumption by up to 90% and energy use by about 50% compared with buildings of similar size and use.​Exhibits inside the centre highlight Stanford Engineering’s history of innovation and technology transfer. These include displays inspired by the garage where Hewlett-Packard began and servers used by Stanford graduate students Sergey Brin and Larry Page while developing the PageRank algorithm that led to Google.​You use AI every day. articles.title: Texas neighbours fought over a five-foot strip beside a Lake Conroe home where meters and a generator crossed the boundary; an appeals court upheld the easement and $100 trespass award
articles.summary: A dispute between two neighbouring families over a five-foot strip of land beside their waterfront homes in Texas reached an appeals court after
articles.body: A dispute between two neighbouring families over a five-foot strip of land beside their waterfront homes in Texas reached an appeals court after disagreements over property boundaries, utility meters, drainage and access for home repairs. The case involved two houses near Lake Conroe, where one property was built so close to the boundary that its owners needed to enter the neighbouring land to maintain it.On Thursday, the Ninth Court of Appeals in Beaumont upheld an earlier ruling that allowed Rudy R. Amador and Carolyn S. Amador to use part of their neighbours' property for repairs and maintenance. According to the judgement document, the court also upheld a $100 award for trespassing against the Amadors, finding that their right to access the land did not extend to unrelated activities.The dispute began when John P. Suitts and Kelly A. Marchman-Suitts, who own Lot 59 in the Pebble Glen on the Lake subdivision, sued the Amadors, owners of adjoining Lot 58. Both properties face Lake Conroe, and the Amadors' house stands less than five inches from the common boundary.The Suitts argued that the Amadors had no written easement allowing them to enter their property or keep equipment extending across the boundary. They also raised concerns about drainage from the neighbouring property and alleged that the Amadors and their contractors had repeatedly entered their land without permission.How the five-foot strip became a disputeThe subdivision's original layout allowed houses to be constructed directly along certain property boundaries. While the Amadors' property had no building setback along the shared boundary, the Suitts' property had a five-foot setback area.The Amadors' house was built in 2003 by its previous owners, Charles and Barbara Rosok. Its gas meter, electric meter and other utility equipment had been installed when the house was constructed. The Amadors purchased the property in 2013 and later installed a Generac generator and related equipment in 2016.According to the Suitts, a 2021 survey showed that the neighbouring property's gas meter, electric meter, Generac panel and gutter extended onto their land. They wanted the equipment removed and sought an order preventing further unauthorised entry.The Amadors argued that access to the five-foot area was necessary because they could not repair or maintain the south side of their house without stepping onto the Suitts' property.What happened between the neighbours?The Suitts accused the Amadors of changing the natural flow of rainwater by raising parts of their backyard and constructing a swimming pool.They also complained about drainage connections, landscaping and incidents involving security lights and survey markers.During the trial, John Suitts testified that Rudy Amador had entered his property without permission and had kicked over a security light and survey stake. Rudy acknowledged entering the property and moving a light. He also admitted kicking survey stakes but claimed he had reacted to an insect crawling up his leg.Rudy received a criminal trespass warning in 2022. He then testified that he stopped entering the property after receiving the warning and instructed his contractors to do the same.However, evidence presented during the trial also showed that the neighbours had previously cooperated. John had allowed drainage connections, helped install a French drain and permitted access for certain maintenance activities.Why the jury recognised an easementThe central legal question was whether the Amadors could claim an easement by estoppel, even though no written easement gave them access to the five-foot strip.An easement allows one person to use another person's land for a specific purpose without owning it. An easement by estoppel can arise when a property owner's words or conduct lead another person to rely on permission to use the land.The jury found that the Amadors had an easement by estoppel for maintaining and repairing the south side of their house. It rejected their claims for easements based on necessity and prior use. The appeals court agreed that sufficient evidence supported the jury's decision.The judges also noted that the Suitts had allowed the previous owners and the Amadors to use the area for approximately 13 years. They had also permitted drainage improvements and participated in some of the work.The court concluded that this conduct supported that the Amadors reasonably relied on being allowed to access the area.Why the court upheld the $100 awardAlthough the Amadors were granted limited access rights, the trial court found that they had trespassed on two occasions.It awarded the Suitts $100 in nominal damages and issued a permanent injunction preventing the Amadors from entering the property for purposes outside the recognised easement.The Suitts also challenged the dismissal of their claims concerning the utility equipment. They argued that every use of the meters, lines and generator panel amounted to a fresh trespass.The appeals court rejected that argument. It found that installing the equipment involved individual acts that caused continuing effects, rather than repeated wrongful acts creating new claims.Because the equipment had been installed years earlier, the court upheld the trial judge's decision that those claims were barred by the applicable limitation period.What the appeals court finally decidedThe appeals court rejected both arguments raised by the Suitts and affirmed the trial court's judgment. The ruling allows the Amadors to access the five-foot setback area for necessary maintenance and repairs to the south side of their house, including its utilities. It does not give them unrestricted permission to enter their neighbours' property.The judgment also leaves in place the $100 trespass award, the restrictions on unrelated entry and the order requiring the Suitts to remove their fence along the south side of their property.You use AI every day. articles.title: Two paintings stolen from Renoir Museum in France are recovered
articles.summary: The two works were seized last month when thieves cut through a fence and smashed a window at the Renoir Museum on the French Riviera.
articles.body:
Two paintings by Auguste Renoir stolen a month ago from a museum in the south of France have been recovered, the local town hall has said.

The two works were seized on 8 September when thieves cut through a fence and smashed a window at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, where the French impressionist had lived during his final years.

The local mayor praised authorities for recovering the paintings and said the news gave immense joy and profound relief.

Six suspects have also been arrested in relation with the heist at Renoir Museum, the town hall confirmed in a statement.

The theft was the latest in a series of high-profile art heists in Europe.

The two missing paintings were the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).

The thieves had used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings inside the museum and had initially made off with four paintings, but dropped two of them in the museum's garden as they fled

"These two paintings are far more than works of art. They are part of our city's history, our cultural heritage and the legacy Auguste Renoir left to Cagnes-sur-Mer," said Mayor Bryan Masson, who is part of France's National Rally.

The town hall said initially that it would provide further details of the recovery on Friday, but cancelled a planned press conference.

The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks.

Opened in 1960, it houses a variety of objects that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters.

Earlier this year paintings by Renoir, Paul Cézanne and Henri Matisse were stolen from a museum near the Italian city of Parma, in a raid that lasted just three minutes. They were recovered in August.

France saw its biggest art robbery in years last October, when crown jewels were stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris.

Disguised as construction workers, the thieves broke into the Louvre's first-floor Apollo Gallery during the museum's opening hours.

They used an angle-grinder to open display cases and made off with €88m (£78m) of jewels that once belonged to France's 19th-Century queens and empresses.

The Louvre was subsequently criticised for under-investing in security.

articles.title: Autism, ADHD and mental health review: What you need to know
articles.summary: It contains big lessons for the NHS, welfare, education and employment policies. What are the key takeaways?
articles.body:
It has been called a "generational opportunity" to rethink support for both mental health conditions and ADHD and autism.

The review, commissioned by then-health secretary Wes Streeting 10 months ago after saying young people were being "over-diagnosed" and "written off", could have major implications for NHS services, the benefits system, schools and employment support.

Its 600-plus pages contain a host of conclusions and recommendations. Here are the key takeaways.

The report is clear that there is an increasing risk of over-diagnosis, but only when it comes to ADHD and autism.

Experts said a rise in diagnoses over the past 25 years meant cases now appear to be outstripping the expected number in the population for some younger age groups.

They gave the example of children aged six to 17 – more than 4% have been diagnosed with autism. That's well above the 1-2% that studies suggest is the true level.

But this comes with a big caveat. There are weaknesses in the data. Evidence about the true level of autism relies on surveys that have not been done for nine years, so the review team have had to estimate what has happened since.

And there are some age groups where these conditions are still being under-diagnosed, and that should not be overlooked.

It is why the review team said it could not yet conclude over-diagnosis was happening "at scale". But there is certainly evidence to suggest we are moving from an era of under-diagnosis to one of over-diagnosis, the experts said.

They warn not every difficulty requires a medical response and there is a risk of blurring the lines between diagnosable ADHD and autism and what should be considered the "normal human variation in brain function, cognition and behaviour".

Where the review team very clearly rejects the idea of over-diagnosis is with mental health. In fact, the chair, Prof Peter Fonagy, has said Streeting was "completely wrong" on that.

He said the increase in mental distress is real – one in four 16 to 24-year-olds are now thought to experience it, up from one in six 30 years ago. He links this to a variety of factors including economic uncertainty, the impact of social media and loss of youth services.

This contrasts with autism and ADHD. While diagnoses have increased, the true level in the whole population (regardless of whether they have come forward or not) has remained broadly stable, according to best estimates.

What is not happening with mental health, though, is an increase in severe mental illness. Population rates of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, for example, have remained stable.

Instead, what is driving the rise is conditions such as anxiety, depression, self-harm and eating disorders.

Where the review experts share, to some extent, Streeting's concerns is on the impact of diagnosis.

They said there was a risk it ends up closing doors to opportunities.

It can, they said, act as a label that defines them by their "difficulties" rather than "strengths and potential".

This then hampers them in education, work and relationships.

Around a third of 16 to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (NEET) report their mental health or autism as a factor.

Those diagnosed with ADHD before the age of 17 are four times more likely to be a NEET than those without.

Addressing this, they said, would require better support post-diagnosis. Some of that is down to the NHS, but as important is the approach of schools, workplaces and wider society.

Another area where the review team is united in its view is that the support system is "falling short" of what people need for both mental health and neurological conditions such as ADHD and autism.

Waiting times for assessment are too long. A third of young people referred to mental health services wait more than a year, while of the 900,000 people waiting for ADHD or autism checks, 90% have waited more than three months.

In the lead up to publication of the report, NHS Alliance, which represents health bosses, said the system was in chaos.

But this goes further than the NHS. The report said support across care, education, employment and welfare remains fragmented, with people having to "jump through hoops" and face repeated assessment and conflicting requirements to get support.

No time should be wasted in tackling these challenges, the review says.

On long waits, it says everyone on a waiting list should be reassessed so that those most in need are prioritised for help. There should no longer be a first-come, first-served approach.

Some of those waiting may benefit from non-medical support, advice about sleeping better or getting more physical exercise, for example. That may even lead to some being removed from the waiting list.

There should also be better assessments before people are placed on waiting lists too. Not every problem needs a medical solution, the experts make clear.

Quality and consistency of autism and ADHD assessments must be improved, with the review highlighting concerns about those done by the private sector on behalf of the NHS. Half of ADHD and a third of autism assessments are done by non-NHS providers, such as charities and private firms.

But they are not subject to the same regulation as NHS providers – and this must change.

The experts also said it wanted to see a ban on direct-to-public advertising of assessments.

The review has said it wants to see action over the next 12 to 24 months. The government has promised to act – and is expected to set out more details in its forthcoming mental health strategy which is expected by the end of the year.

articles.title: King pays Andrew's £1.5m repair bill on Royal Lodge
articles.summary: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor was charged £1.5m in repair and restoration costs after surrendering the lease on the 30-room mansion.
articles.body:
King Charles has paid Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's £1.5m repair bill that's owed for the poor condition of Mountbatten-Windsor's former home at Royal Lodge in Windsor.

It's understood that the money is coming from the King's private income - and will cover what Andrew owes his former landlords, the Crown Estate, on leaving Royal Lodge.

There was a total £1.8m penalty for the "dilapidations" to Royal Lodge, but that has been reduced by the £300,000 Mountbatten-Windsor would have received for an early surrender of his lease.

The Crown Estate say they have not given any money to Mountbatten-Windsor at the conclusion of his lease and have now received the net £1.5m payment they were owed.

Why did Andrew leave Windsor's Royal Lodge in such a hurry?

Andrew moves out of Royal Lodge home early after latest Epstein files

Mountbatten-Windsor left his Royal Lodge home in February, in the middle of a storm of revelations about his connections to the US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

He has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.

The former Prince Andrew was moved to Sandringham, with his brother the King using his own money to provide his upkeep and accommodation.

Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested later that month on suspicion of misconduct in public office - and a court ruling on Thursday found fault with the search warrants used by the police.

But despite moving to Sandringham, Mountbatten-Windsor's lease on Royal Lodge had remained until October - and as that officially ends, the Crown Estate is revealing the terms on which it concluded.

When Andrew had taken on the 75 year lease in 2003, he had made considerable up-front payments, including about £7.5m for repairs, which meant that he did not have to pay a monthly rent.

It also meant that if he gave up the lease within the first 25 years he would be legally entitled to some compensation - with that amount reducing each year.

Leaving in October 2026 would have meant that the Crown Estate would have had to pay him back about £302,000.

However that amount has been overshadowed by what he owes to the landlord for the state of the building - and so the Crown Estate says it has now received a net amount of £1.5m.

It's understood that the payment of that money by the King is to avoid leaving the Crown Estate out of pocket.

Whether Mountbatten-Windsor will repay his brother is said to be a private matter - and there are no further details of what this might say about Andrew's personal finances.

There was also no comment on how the King feels about this arrangement - and there is said to be no connection between this payment and the King making clear this week that his financial support should not go to cover Andrew's legal costs in his battle over search warrants.

It has so far not been decided how the 30-room mansion in Windsor will be used in future, but it is expected to be used to deliver a commercial return - and at present there are no plans for another royal occupant.

"The lease for Royal Lodge has ended and our focus now is firmly on its future use and the opportunities to generate additional financial value for the nation from its early return," said a Crown Estate spokesperson.

A report by the National Audit Office had revealed earlier this year that Mountbatten-Windsor had been sub-letting buildings at Royal Lodge, although the amount was never revealed.

That report from the public spending watchdog also showed that Andrew's daughters, Princess Beatrice and Eugenie, had accommodation inside royal palaces which they did not pay for, with the cost being covered privately by the King.

articles.title: Mick Foley raised and donated over $40,000 to help wrestlers facing financial hardship; his shirt auctions support the Cauliflower Alley Club’s benevolent fund
articles.summary: Professional wrestling is built on punishing travel, physical tolls and independent contracts, so when injury, illness or age catches up with a performer,
articles.body: Professional wrestling is built on punishing travel, physical tolls and independent contracts, so when injury, illness or age catches up with a performer, the safety net can be thin. Mick Foley, the Hardcore Legend, has spent years strengthening that net. Through auctions, appearances and personal donations, he has channelled generosity into the Cauliflower Alley Club, the nonprofit organisation that helps wrestlers in need. This article traces the club's mission, the more than $40,000 Foley has raised, his nightly shirt auction, his charitable record, and the honours that recognise him, showing why his giving matters to the wrestling family.What the Cauliflower Alley Club does: A benevolent fund for wrestlersThe Cauliflower Alley Club’s purpose today is clear, the club's mission is to financially assist those in the wrestling industry facing difficult financial times, and it keeps applications confidential. Professional Wrestling Stories adds that the club has distributed over one million dollars through its Benevolent Fund to wrestlers and industry workers facing hardship, calling that fund its core function. Money for the fund is raised largely through the annual reunion weekend. That work matters because many wrestlers are independent contractors who may lack strong insurance or medical coverage, a point made by Casanova in SlamWrestling.Mick Foley raises over $40,000, how the Goodwill Ambassador's generosity supports wrestlers in needOn July 17, 2026, the Cauliflower Alley Club published an announcement celebrating Mick Foley's generosity. The post contrasts celebrities who merely attach their names to causes with Foley, who it says has devoted real heart to this one. As the club's Goodwill Ambassador and the namesake of the Mick Foley Philanthropy Award, he continues to lead by example. According to the club, over the past year alone he has personally raised and donated more than $40,000 to help it provide financial assistance to members of the professional wrestling community during times of need. The club adds that Foley has never sought recognition for his generosity, yet accomplishments like this deserve celebration. They credit his compassion, selflessness and commitment to giving back with touching countless lives, and they are thankful for his dedication to the wrestling family.The shirt-off-my-back auction: How Mick Foley turns every stage show into a fundraiser for wrestlersFoley's fundraising is not limited to announcements. Fightful reports that at every show on his "40 Years of Foley" stage tour, he auctions off the shirt he is wearing, with the proceeds going to the Cauliflower Alley Club's fund for wrestlers in need. In an Instagram message quoted by Fightful, Foley said the nightly auction had raised more than $40,000. During the United Kingdom leg, a winning bid of nine hundred pounds, worth over a thousand dollars, was placed in Birmingham, England, but two bidders left without paying. Several audience members stepped in with donations, and $600 still reached the club. Fightful later updated its report to say the two men donated $1,000, and Foley said he believes in second chances.Mick Foley's wider charity record: Make-A-Wish events, anti-abuse advocacy and child sponsorship supportThe National Wrestling Hall of Fame, which honoured Foley with its Frank Gotch Award in 2010, observes that some of his finest achievements happened away from the ring. Its biography notes that Foley has participated in numerous Make-A-Wish Foundation events, is an active member of the Rape, Abuse and Incest National Network, and is one of the leading donors of Child Fund International. The Hall of Fame concludes that his charitable contributions have brought positive recognition to professional wrestling. Seen alongside the Cauliflower Alley Club fundraising, this record shows a pattern rather than a single campaign, Foley supports young people, survivors of abuse and fellow wrestlers alike, applying the same personal commitment to each cause. For readers wondering why the wrestling community values him so highly, this breadth of giving offers part of the answer.Awards honouring Mick Foley and wider recognitionRecognition from the club runs deep. According to the club, Foley was presented with the Iron Mike Mazurki Award at the 2025 reunion, an honour that celebrates people who have transcended wrestling through crossover achievements. It is the club's highest honour and lists Foley as the 2025 winner. Speaking to the Kayfabe Friends Wrestling Podcast at the event, Foley said he is grateful to be respected by different generations, and the outlet noted that the club's cause is one he is happy to support. These tributes show a relationship built over many years.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Govt orders internet shutdown within 4-kilometer radius of Janpath–Kartavya Path ahead of anti-CEC protest
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The government on Friday allowed the temporary suspension of internet services within a 4-kilometer radius around the Janpath–Kartavya Path
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The government on Friday allowed the temporary suspension of internet services within a 4-kilometer radius around the Janpath–Kartavya Path crossing. The decision is part of the Delhi Police's preventive measures taken in view of the protests being called by various outfits, including the opposition Congres-led INDIA bloc and the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)."Internet services will remain suspended within a 4-kilometer radius around the Janpath–Kartavya Path crossing. Services will remain suspended from 10 PM on October 9 to 10 PM on October 10. Instructions have been issued to suspend all forms of mobile internet technology," the notice said.Senior Delhi Police officers on Friday also held a high-level meeting at the police headquarters to review the law-and-order situation ahead CJP's proposed protest at Jantar Mantar.The meeting focused on assessing the security situation and reviewing arrangements to maintain law and order in the national capital, they said.Officers also examined recent observations made by the Supreme Court, which are expected to feature in the discussions, sources added.The planned protest has prompted heightened security preparations across Delhi.Of the 13 Delhi-bound trains cancelled by the North Western Railway for Saturday ahead of the protest, most are from Haryana.Though the railways cited “operational reasons” for the cancellation, the move comes ahead of the protests called by the Cockroach Janata Party and other groups in Delhi on October 10, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over controversy surrounding the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.On Friday, the Bikaner Division of North Western Railway announced the cancellation of 13 train services bound for Delhi.Delhi Police also proposed closing entry and exit gates at 57 metro stations across the national capital and reducing train frequency at these stations.Hours after the measures disrupting the railways & metro adopted, the Supreme Court orally asked the Centre to ensure that Delhi Metro operations are not completely suspended ahead of the protest, stressing that preventive measures should not cause inconvenience to ordinary commuters.A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana expressed concern over the scheduled closure of 57 Metro stations, observing that the restrictions could affect students, employees and other people dependent on public transport."We are concerned with closure of metro services," the CJI-led Bench remarked, addressing Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, who appeared for the Centre."One very important principle that we follow for every citizen is the principle of proportionality… You have to prevent certain things. Take measures only to the extent necessary to prevent them. But that does not mean you use a hammer to kill a fly. That principle must be kept in mind," CJI Kant further told Mehta.The solicitor general said he understands the concerns of the court and will discuss with the authorities concerned, but said that the remark of the CJI on use of a hammer was just an example and it should not be reported that the Chief Justice of India told the government that it is using a hammer to kill a fly.CJI Kant said, "Exercise caution in abundance. There is nothing wrong with that."Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Rancho Cariñoso was listed for $100 million in 2021 and $109 million in 2022; four years later, the 4.2-acre California beachfront horse ranch went to auction with bidding opening at $20 million
articles.summary: Not many properties on the Southern California coast have seen their asking prices change as much as Rancho Cariñoso.
articles.body: Not many properties on the Southern California coast have seen their asking prices change as much as Rancho Cariñoso. The extraordinary 4.2-acre oceanfront ranch estate along Padaro Lane in Santa Barbara County’s seaside city of Carpinteria was first listed in 2021 for $100 million, Mansion Global reported. A year later, in 2022, the price rose to $109 million. The asking price subsequently fell to $70 million in September 2024 before dropping further to $48.975 million. Now, four years after it first came on the market, the ranch has gone to auction, with bidding starting at $20 million.Ranch land on the bluffsThe estate has nearly one acre of private beach. The property also has a horse trail that runs from the grounds straight to the sand. The land is zoned for nine horses. Loon Point, a surf break that draws experienced surfers, lies nearby. The ranch also has a single-storey house, which was built in 2014. It has three bedrooms, 3.5 bathrooms and 2,514 square feet of living space. There is a fireplace in the living room, along with large windows overlooking the outdoors. A workshop and garage stand apart from the main house.Owners opt for an auctionThe Cameron family has owned the land for more than four decades. In 1978, the family bought the original property, which covered nearly 28 acres, for $1 million, according to the New York Post. Concierge Auctions ran the sale online. Barron and Tessa Hilton of Compass California were the listing agents.Rancho Cariñoso “offers a lifestyle that cannot be replicated or rebuilt”, according to Chad Roffers, CEO and co-founder of Concierge Auctions. “The Southern California coastline has been developed for generations, and true beachfront ranch estates of this scale do not come to market anymore.”“What makes Rancho Cariñoso so rare isn’t any single feature – it’s the combination. Where else in Southern California can you ride horses directly onto the beach, anchor a yacht offshore, surf a private break, and retreat to four acres of complete oceanfront privacy? That is what makes this a once-in-a-generation offering, and we’re thrilled to introduce it to buyers around the world alongside Concierge Auctions,” Barron Hilton said.On 4 September, Concierge Auctions announced that bidding had opened at $20 million. An auction opening price is a starting point, not a final figure. The property record now lists the ranch at $20 million, with its status marked as pending. The record does not say whether that figure is the final sale price.The buyer would gain exclusive access to Padaro Lane, known for its wealthy residents. In 2024, Ellen DeGeneres sold her neighbouring oceanfront property for $96 million. Actor Kevin Costner also owns an estate on the same bluffs. Celebrities such as George Lucas, Mila Kunis, Ashton Kutcher and Kourtney Kardashian also have homes nearby in the Padaro Lane and Montecito areas. Privacy and direct access to the coast draw wealthy buyers to the area.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: 'Inevitable': AI companies preparing for catastrophic event in 6-12 months, claims report
articles.summary: AI companies are preparing for a potential catastrophic AI incident in the next 6-12 months, which executives fear could trigger a massive public backlash
articles.body: AI companies are preparing for a potential catastrophic AI incident in the next 6-12 months, which executives fear could trigger a massive public backlash and force governments to impose sweeping regulations, Axios reported.The executives are gaming out worst-case scenarios, including cyberattacks that could disrupt financial services, internet connectivity, electricity and water supplies. According to Axios, several industry insiders believe a major incident could occur within the next six to 12 months, potentially turning an already sceptical public against AI companies and their leaders, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei."OpenAI conducts preparedness exercises where teams discuss and work through a range of potential scenarios," an OpenAI spokesperson told Axios. "These scenarios are not treated as inevitable, but are meant to help us prepare for a variety of circumstances." Anthropic declined to comment.Artificial intelligence agents developed by OpenAI have reportedly bypassed security restrictions, probed government websites and attempted to obscure their activities, raising concerns about the risks posed by increasingly autonomous AI systems.Cybersecurity researchers at Asymmetric Security said their investigation identified activity involving at least 55 additional websites between March and September, including those of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the International Energy Agency and the Mayo Clinic. The researchers reported finding evidence of attempts to evade sandbox restrictions and conceal activity records.Companies seek to shape future regulationHowever, the prospect of regulation remains complicated by the strategic competition between the United States and China. US President Donald Trump has rejected calls to slow AI development, arguing that tighter restrictions could allow Beijing to gain an advantage.The enormous economic stakes also make a slowdown difficult. With substantial investments flowing into data centres, computing infrastructure and advanced models, any sudden restrictions could disrupt businesses and affect an economy increasingly dependent on AI.Some proposed safeguards include independent evaluations, stronger oversight and mandatory kill switches for advanced systems. However, experts have questioned whether shutting down AI systems across the industry would be feasible, particularly as open-weight models can be downloaded and used without direct oversight from their developers.The central concern for AI executives is that a catastrophic incident could force policymakers to act before the industry and governments have agreed on effective safeguards. The preparations are aimed at influencing that response before a crisis, rather than waiting for one to determine the future of AI regulation.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
